title: The Long-Term Study Roadmap
useCase: Planning a multi-month study schedule for a major standardized test.
promptText: I am preparing for a major exam ([Insert Exam, e.g., GATE CSE]) which is [Insert Number] months away. Create a comprehensive, week-by-week roadmap. Break down the core subjects (like [Insert Subjects, e.g., Data Structures, OS, DBMS]), allocate time based on topic weight and difficulty, and include specific milestones for completing previous year questions (PYQs) and mock tests.
proTip: Use this as your master blueprint. You can ask the AI to regenerate specific weeks if you fall behind.

title: The Feynman Concept Breakdown
useCase: Mastering difficult theoretical concepts.
promptText: Explain [Insert Concept, e.g., Paging and Segmentation] using the Feynman Technique. Start with a very simple analogy. Then, explain it again using the proper technical terminology required for an exam. Finally, give me a challenging scenario-based question to test if I actually understand it.
proTip: Don't just read the explanation—actually try to answer the test question at the end.

title: The Active Recall Generator
useCase: Creating flashcards or self-test questions from textbook notes.
promptText: I am pasting my notes on [Insert Topic] below. Generate 10 difficult 'Active Recall' questions based on this text. Format the output with the questions first. Put the answers at the very bottom of the response so I am forced to guess them before checking. Notes: [Insert Notes]
proTip: Active recall is scientifically proven to be more effective than just re-reading your notes.

title: The Weakness Diagnoser
useCase: Understanding why you keep getting a specific type of question wrong.
promptText: I am struggling with [Insert Topic, e.g., finding the time complexity of recursive algorithms]. Here is a problem I got wrong: [Insert Problem], and here was my thought process/answer: [Insert Your Answer]. Do not just give me the correct answer. Tell me exactly where my fundamental misunderstanding lies and explain the core rule I am forgetting.
proTip: This turns the AI into a personalized tutor that fixes the root cause of your mistakes.

title: The Theorem & Formula Explainer
useCase: Memorizing complex formulas by understanding their derivations.
promptText: I need to memorize [Insert Formula/Theorem, e.g., Master Theorem or Bayes' Theorem] for an exam. Break down this formula part by part. What does each variable represent in plain English? Explain the intuition behind why this formula works, rather than just giving me the mathematical proof.
proTip: Understanding the 'why' makes remembering the 'what' much easier during a stressful exam.

title: The Past-Paper Pattern Analyzer
useCase: Identifying high-yield topics from past exam questions.
promptText: Here are 5 essay questions/problems from previous years' exams on the subject of [Insert Subject]: [Insert Questions]. Analyze these questions and tell me what specific core concepts the examiner is clearly prioritizing. What should I focus my remaining study time on based on these patterns?
proTip: Examiners often test the same core principles using different wrappers. This finds the core.

title: The 'Cheat Sheet' Synthesizer
useCase: Condensing a massive chapter into a one-page review sheet.
promptText: I need to create a 1-page quick-review cheat sheet for [Insert Topic, e.g., Sorting Algorithms]. Extract the absolute most important definitions, rules, time/space complexities, and edge cases. Format this as a highly structured, dense markdown table or bulleted list.
proTip: Review this generated cheat sheet 30 minutes before walking into the exam hall.

title: The Concept Comparator
useCase: Distinguishing between two very similar concepts that confuse you.
promptText: I always get confused between [Concept A, e.g., Mutex] and [Concept B, e.g., Semaphore]. Create a strict comparison table highlighting their differences in definition, use-case, and limitations. Then, give me a trick or mnemonic to remember which is which.
proTip: Comparing two things forces your brain to categorize them, preventing mix-ups on multiple-choice tests.

title: The Edge-Case Tester
useCase: Preparing for trick questions designed to trap students.
promptText: I understand the basics of [Insert Topic, e.g., Binary Search Trees]. Now, I want you to test me on the edge cases. Give me 3 tricky, exception-to-the-rule scenarios that professors love to put on advanced exams to trip up students.
proTip: This prepares you for the hardest 10% of the exam that separates top scorers from the rest.

title: The Explain-Like-I'm-5 (ELI5)
useCase: Breaking through a mental block on a confusing topic.
promptText: I am completely stuck on [Insert Topic, e.g., Neural Network Backpropagation]. Explain it to me like I am 5 years old. Use zero jargon. Use a real-world, physical analogy that a child could understand.
proTip: Use this when you hit a wall. You can ask it to slowly increase the academic level once you grasp the ELI5 version.

title: The Spaced Repetition Scheduler
useCase: Optimizing review times to combat the forgetting curve.
promptText: I just finished studying [Insert Topic]. I have an exam on [Insert Date]. Design a spaced repetition study schedule for this specific topic leading up to the exam. Tell me exactly which dates I need to review this material to maximize long-term retention.
proTip: Pair this with a calendar app to automate your review reminders.

title: The Multiple-Choice Trap Finder
useCase: Learning how to eliminate distractor answers.
promptText: Generate a highly difficult multiple-choice question about [Insert Topic]. Include 4 options. Make sure 2 of the incorrect options are 'distractors'—answers that look right if you make a common mistake. After I guess, explain the psychology behind why those distractors were chosen.
proTip: Improves your test-taking strategy, not just your subject knowledge.

title: The Mnemonic Generator
useCase: Memorizing long lists or orders of operations.
promptText: I need to memorize this exact list in order: [Insert List, e.g., The 7 layers of the OSI model]. Create 3 different memorable mnemonics for this. Make one funny, make one logical, and make one bizarre.
proTip: The more ridiculous the mnemonic, the easier it is to remember under pressure.

title: The Blank-Page Braindump Assessor
useCase: Testing true, unassisted recall.
promptText: I just did a 'braindump' where I wrote down everything I know about [Insert Topic] from memory. Here is my text: [Insert Text]. Review my braindump. Tell me what key information I completely forgot to include, and correct any factual errors I made.
proTip: Do a braindump on a blank sheet of paper, type it up quickly, and use this prompt to find your blind spots.

title: The Theory-to-Application Bridge
useCase: Preparing for application-based exam questions.
promptText: I know the theory behind [Insert Concept, e.g., Object-Oriented Programming Principles]. Now, give me a practical, real-world engineering problem where I have to apply this theory to solve it. Grade my approach once I respond.
proTip: Crucial for university-level exams that test application over rote memorization.

title: The Time-Crunch Simulator
useCase: Practicing speed and accuracy for timed tests.
promptText: Act as a timed exam simulator. Give me 5 rapid-fire questions on [Insert Topic]. I will answer them all at once. My goal is to answer them in under [Insert Time, e.g., 3 minutes]. Go.
proTip: Use this to overcome test anxiety and get used to retrieving information quickly.

title: The Grading Rubric Reverse-Engineer
useCase: Writing better subjective/essay answers.
promptText: I have to write an essay/long-form answer on [Insert Topic]. If you were the strict professor grading this, what specific keywords, structural elements, and arguments would you require to give this a perfect 10/10? Provide the ideal grading rubric.
proTip: Write your answer specifically to satisfy the generated rubric.

title: The 'Devil's Advocate' Debater
useCase: Deepening understanding by defending your knowledge.
promptText: I believe that [Insert Statement/Fact, e.g., normalization is always required in database design]. Play devil's advocate and argue aggressively against my point. I will defend my stance, and you will grade how well I hold up against your arguments.
proTip: Defending a concept solidifies it in your memory far better than passive reading.

title: The Study Session Warm-Up
useCase: Getting into the zone before a long study block.
promptText: I am about to start a 2-hour study session on [Insert Subject]. Ask me 3 quick, easy, fundamental questions to warm up my brain and get me into the context of the subject.
proTip: Prevents the 'blank stare' when you first open your textbook.

title: The Exam Day Strategy Coach
useCase: Planning how to tackle the actual test paper.
promptText: My exam is structured like this: [Insert Structure, e.g., 65 questions, 3 hours, negative marking for wrong answers]. What is the mathematically and psychologically optimal strategy for navigating this paper? How should I allocate my time, and when should I guess vs. skip?
proTip: A good strategy can save you points even if you don't know all the answers.

title: The Socratic Debugger
useCase: Finding logic errors without the AI just giving you the answer.
promptText: Here is my [Insert Language, e.g., Python] code: [Insert Code]. It is supposed to [Insert Expected Output], but it is doing [Insert Actual Output]. Act as a Socratic tutor. Do NOT rewrite the code for me. Instead, ask me a guiding question that points me toward the line where my logic is failing.
proTip: This builds actual problem-solving muscles instead of relying on AI as a crutch.

title: The Big O Analyzer
useCase: Optimizing algorithmic efficiency for interviews or competitive programming.
promptText: Analyze the time and space complexity of my following [Insert Language] code: [Insert Code]. Break down exactly why it has this complexity step-by-step. Then, suggest one way I could refactor this to optimize its Big O performance, and explain the trade-offs of that optimization.
proTip: Crucial for passing technical interviews where brute-force solutions aren't enough.

title: The Stack Trace Translator
useCase: Deciphering massive, intimidating error logs.
promptText: I am getting this error traceback in my [Insert Framework/Language] application: [Insert Stack Trace]. Translate this error into plain English. What is the root cause, which specific line of my code triggered it, and what are the top 3 most common reasons this error occurs?
proTip: Saves you 30 minutes of scrolling through Stack Overflow trying to match your exact error.

title: The Clean Code Refactorer
useCase: Making messy code professional and readable.
promptText: Here is a working piece of [Insert Language] code: [Insert Code]. It works, but it is messy. Refactor this code to follow standard industry best practices (like PEP 8 for Python or SOLID principles). Explain every change you made and why it makes the code more maintainable.
proTip: Use this before pushing code to a repository or adding it to your personal portfolio.

title: The Language Rosetta Stone
useCase: Translating logic from a language you know to one you are learning.
promptText: I know how to write this logic in [Insert Known Language, e.g., Java]: [Insert Code]. I am trying to learn [Insert Target Language, e.g., Python]. Translate this exact logic into idiomatic [Target Language]. Highlight any language-specific features you used that don't exist in the original language.
proTip: The fastest way to learn a new language is to map it directly to one you already understand.

title: The ML Model Diagnoser
useCase: Figuring out why a machine learning model is performing poorly.
promptText: I am training a [Insert Model Type, e.g., Random Forest / Neural Network] for [Insert Task, e.g., emotion detection / prediction]. My training accuracy is [Insert %] but my validation accuracy is [Insert %]. Based on this, diagnose what might be happening (e.g., overfitting, data leakage) and suggest 3 specific hyperparameter adjustments or data preprocessing steps I should try.
proTip: Helps you stop blindly tweaking parameters and start tuning with a strategy.

title: The SQL Query Optimizer
useCase: Speeding up slow database queries.
promptText: Here is my database schema: [Insert Schema details]. I am running this SQL query: [Insert Query]. It is taking too long to execute. Explain how the database engine is likely processing this query, and rewrite it to be more efficient. Suggest any indexes I should add.
proTip: Essential for backend web development and database management system (DBMS) exams.

title: The Regex Demystifier
useCase: Understanding or writing complex Regular Expressions.
promptText: I need a Regular Expression in [Insert Language] to match the following pattern: [Describe Pattern, e.g., valid email addresses ending in .edu]. Write the regex and break it down character-by-character so I understand exactly how it works. Provide 3 matching test cases and 3 failing test cases.
proTip: Never blindly copy-paste Regex again. This forces you to understand the syntax.

title: The Edge-Case Hunter
useCase: Preventing your app from breaking in production.
promptText: Here is a function I wrote to handle [Insert Task]: [Insert Code]. Act as a QA tester trying to break my code. List 5 weird, obscure edge-cases or unexpected inputs that would cause this function to fail, crash, or return incorrect data.
proTip: Run your core logic through this before calling a project 'finished'.

title: The Unit Test Generator
useCase: Quickly scaffolding test suites for your functions.
promptText: Here is my [Insert Language] function: [Insert Code]. Write a complete suite of unit tests for this function using [Insert Testing Framework, e.g., PyTest or JUnit]. Include tests for the happy path, edge cases, and expected exceptions.
proTip: Writing tests is tedious. Let the AI write the boilerplate so you can focus on the logic.

title: The Architecture Critic
useCase: Validating the structure of a new full-stack project.
promptText: I am planning to build a [Insert Project, e.g., personal portfolio with a 3D model showcase]. I plan to use [Insert Tech Stack, e.g., React, Three.js, Node.js]. Critique this architecture. What are the potential bottlenecks? Is there a lighter-weight alternative I should consider for this specific use case?
proTip: Measure twice, cut once. Use this before setting up your repository.

title: The UI/CSS Fixer
useCase: Solving frustrating frontend layout issues.
promptText: I am trying to build a [Insert UI Element, e.g., responsive navigation bar] using [Insert CSS Framework, e.g., Tailwind CSS / Vanilla CSS]. I want it to [Describe desired look], but currently it is [Describe issue]. Here is my code: [Insert Code]. Tell me which CSS property is causing the conflict and how to fix it.
proTip: Saves hours of blindly changing 'flex' and 'absolute' properties.

title: The Explain-Like-I'm-5 Code Reader
useCase: Understanding complex open-source code or a teammate's pull request.
promptText: I am reading this piece of code and I don't understand how it works: [Insert Code]. Go through it line-by-line and explain what it is doing in plain, non-technical English. What is the ultimate goal of this block of code?
proTip: Great for learning advanced techniques by reverse-engineering other people's code.

title: The Design Pattern Matcher
useCase: Applying Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) concepts correctly.
promptText: I am building a system that needs to [Describe the problem, e.g., notify multiple users when a database updates]. What standard software design pattern (e.g., Observer, Singleton, Factory) is best suited for this problem? Explain how the pattern works in this context and give a skeleton code example in [Insert Language].
proTip: Elevates your code from 'scripting' to professional 'software engineering'.

title: The API Integration Planner
useCase: Connecting your app to external services safely.
promptText: I need to integrate the [Insert API Name, e.g., Stripe / TMDB] API into my [Insert Language] backend. Outline the exact steps I need to take. Include how to securely store the API keys, handle rate limiting, and write a basic fetch/request block with proper error handling.
proTip: Treats API documentation like a clear, actionable checklist.

title: The Git Rescue Mission
useCase: Fixing terrifying version control mistakes.
promptText: I messed up my Git repository. I accidentally [Describe mistake, e.g., committed sensitive data / merged the wrong branch]. Here is the current state of my branches and my last few commands: [Insert Context]. Give me the exact, safe terminal commands to undo this without losing my actual code changes.
proTip: Always read the explanation of the Git commands before running them so you learn how to fix it next time.

title: The Code Documenter
useCase: Generating professional comments and docstrings.
promptText: Here is a completed [Insert Language] script: [Insert Code]. Add professional, industry-standard docstrings and inline comments. Explain the parameters, return types, and the general logic flow without cluttering the file with obvious comments.
proTip: Makes your GitHub portfolio look highly professional to recruiters.

title: The Security Auditor
useCase: Finding vulnerabilities before deploying.
promptText: Review this [Insert Language] code handling user input/authentication: [Insert Code]. Act as a cybersecurity auditor. Identify any potential vulnerabilities (like SQL injection, XSS, or improper token handling) and show me exactly how to patch them.
proTip: Never deploy web applications handling user data without running a basic security check.

title: The 'Will It Scale?' Tester
useCase: Thinking beyond the local development environment.
promptText: My code currently works for 100 users: [Insert Code or Architecture outline]. What will break, slow down, or crash if this suddenly gets 100,000 concurrent users? Identify the architectural bottlenecks and suggest scalable solutions (e.g., caching, load balancing).
proTip: Excellent mental exercise for system design interviews.

title: The Variable Naming Assistant
useCase: Solving the hardest problem in computer science: naming things.
promptText: I have a function that [Describe what the function does]. It takes variables currently named 'x', 'y', and 'data'. Suggest 5 sets of highly descriptive, clean-code variable and function names that make the code self-documenting.
proTip: Good naming conventions eliminate the need for excessive comments.

title: The Resume Roaster
useCase: Getting a brutally honest critique of your resume before applying.
promptText: Act as a ruthless, senior technical recruiter for a top-tier tech company. Review my resume below. Tear it apart. Point out every weak action verb, vague metric, and formatting flaw. Do not hold back. Then, give me 3 actionable steps to make my top project sound more impressive. Resume: [Insert Resume Text]
proTip: It’s better to get 'roasted' by an AI in private than rejected by an ATS tracker in public.

title: The STAR Method Coach
useCase: Structuring perfect behavioral interview answers.
promptText: I am preparing for a behavioral interview for a [Insert Role, e.g., Software Developer] position. Ask me a common behavioral question (like 'Tell me about a time you failed'). I will provide a rough answer. Then, rewrite my answer using the strict STAR framework (Situation, Task, Action, Result) and tell me what critical details I forgot to include.
proTip: The STAR method is the industry standard. Use this prompt to train your brain to speak in that format automatically.

title: The Mock Technical Interviewer
useCase: Simulating a high-pressure technical screening.
promptText: Act as a Hiring Manager interviewing me for a [Insert Role, e.g., Machine Learning Engineer] role. The core technologies required are [Insert Tech, e.g., Python, TensorFlow, SQL]. Ask me one technical interview question at a time. Wait for my answer. Critique my logic, point out edge cases I missed, and then ask a follow-up question. Do not break character.
proTip: Treat this exactly like a real interview. Type your answers without looking up documentation.

title: The Project Impact Quantifier
useCase: Translating simple coding projects into business value.
promptText: I built a project: [Describe Project, e.g., an Emotion Detection System using ML]. Right now, my resume just says 'Built an app using Python'. Help me quantify the impact of this project. Give me 5 examples of impressive, metric-driven bullet points I could use, assuming realistic benchmarks for performance, accuracy, or efficiency.
proTip: Recruiters look for numbers and impact, not just a list of the programming languages you used.

title: The ATS Keyword Scanner
useCase: Tailoring your resume to a specific job description to beat the bots.
promptText: Here is a job description I want to apply for: [Insert Job Description]. And here is my current resume: [Insert Resume Text]. Identify the top 10 core keywords and skills missing from my resume that the Applicant Tracking System (ATS) will be looking for. Suggest where I can naturally weave them into my existing experience.
proTip: Never lie to an ATS, but always use the exact terminology the job posting uses (e.g., 'API Integration' vs 'Connected APIs').

title: The System Design Simulator
useCase: Practicing architecture rounds for mid-level or senior roles.
promptText: Give me a classic System Design interview prompt (e.g., Design Twitter, Design a global URL shortener). I will outline the high-level architecture, database schema, and scaling strategy. Act as the interviewer and challenge my design, specifically questioning my choices regarding load balancing, database scaling, and latency.
proTip: Focus on the trade-offs. The AI will push back; be prepared to defend why you chose NoSQL over SQL, for instance.

title: The Portfolio Elevator Pitch
useCase: Explaining complex personal projects succinctly to non-technical recruiters.
promptText: I need a 30-second elevator pitch for my portfolio project: [Describe Project, e.g., an IPL Match Prediction Model]. Write three versions of this pitch: One for a highly technical Engineering Manager, one for a non-technical HR Recruiter, and one for a casual networking event.
proTip: Knowing your audience is critical. You shouldn't explain hyperparameter tuning to an HR recruiter.

title: The 'Tell Me About Yourself' Sculptor
useCase: Nailing the first and most important question of any interview.
promptText: I am applying for [Insert Target Role]. Here is a messy brain-dump of my background, education, and passions: [Insert Background]. Distill this into a powerful, 90-second 'Tell me about yourself' narrative. It should highlight my trajectory, why I am passionate about this field, and end with why I am excited about this specific role.
proTip: The goal is a cohesive narrative, not a chronological reading of your resume.

title: The Whiteboard Coder
useCase: Practicing algorithmic problem solving without an IDE.
promptText: Give me a medium-difficulty LeetCode-style problem related to [Insert Topic, e.g., Trees, Dynamic Programming]. I will write the solution in plain text. Act as the interviewer: analyze my time/space complexity, point out syntax errors I'd normally rely on an IDE to catch, and suggest optimal refactors.
proTip: Whiteboard coding tests your thought process more than your syntax memory. Explain your logic as you type.

title: The 'I Don't Know' Strategist
useCase: Handling interview questions you have no idea how to answer gracefully.
promptText: I am in a technical interview and the interviewer just asked me a question about [Insert Obscure Topic] that I do not know the answer to. Give me 3 professional ways to pivot, admit I don't know the exact answer, but showcase my problem-solving process to figure it out.
proTip: Saying 'I don't know, but here is how I would find out' is infinitely better than freezing or lying.

title: The Cold Outreach Crafter
useCase: Networking with alumni or engineers on LinkedIn.
promptText: I want to send a cold LinkedIn message to a [Insert Role, e.g., Senior Developer] at [Insert Company]. I am a student looking for a short informational interview, NOT asking for a job directly. Write a concise, 4-sentence outreach message that is highly personalized, respectful of their time, and has a clear call to action.
proTip: Keep it short. Busy professionals ignore long walls of text from strangers.

title: The Salary Negotiator
useCase: Practicing the most uncomfortable conversation in the hiring process.
promptText: I have received a job offer for [Insert Role] offering [Insert Salary]. Based on market research, I want to ask for [Insert Target Salary]. Act as the HR representative. I will pitch my counter-offer. You will push back with a common HR objection (e.g., 'budget constraints'). Let's roleplay the negotiation.
proTip: Roleplaying this reduces the anxiety of doing it for real. Always anchor your negotiation in the value you bring, not your personal expenses.

title: The Reverse Interviewer
useCase: Asking the employer high-quality questions at the end of the interview.
promptText: I am interviewing for a [Insert Role] at a [Insert Company Type, e.g., fast-paced startup / large enterprise]. Generate 5 highly insightful, non-generic questions I can ask the interviewer at the end. These questions should help me uncover the real engineering culture, work-life balance, and tech debt.
proTip: An interview is a two-way street. Asking insightful questions proves you are evaluating them just as hard as they are evaluating you.

title: The Tech Stack Defender
useCase: Explaining why you chose specific tools for your personal projects.
promptText: In my portfolio, I built a [Insert Project, e.g., recipe website] using [Insert Tech Stack, e.g., React and Node.js]. Play the role of a skeptical Senior Engineer. Grill me on why I chose those specific tools over alternatives (like Vue or Django). I will defend my choices, and you will grade my reasoning.
proTip: 'Because I saw it in a tutorial' is not a valid answer. You must learn to articulate engineering trade-offs.

title: The Behavioral Red Flag Checker
useCase: Ensuring your answers don't accidentally make you look difficult to work with.
promptText: Here is my drafted answer to the interview question 'Tell me about a time you had a conflict with a teammate': [Insert Answer]. Analyze this answer. Does it contain any hidden 'red flags'? Do I sound too defensive, arrogant, or passive? Suggest tweaks to make me sound collaborative and mature.
proTip: Self-awareness is key. You never want to sound like you are blaming others, even if they were in the wrong.

title: The Transition Storyteller
useCase: Explaining a pivot from one field or major to another.
promptText: My background is in [Insert Previous Field/Major], but I am applying for jobs in [Insert New Field, e.g., Software Engineering]. Help me craft a compelling narrative that connects the two. What transferable skills from my past make me uniquely valuable in my new chosen career path?
proTip: Don't hide your past; leverage it. Diverse backgrounds often bring unique problem-solving perspectives.

title: The Take-Home Assignment Reviewer
useCase: Sanity-checking a technical challenge before submission.
promptText: I completed a take-home coding assignment for a job application. The prompt was [Insert Prompt]. Here is my core logic/code: [Insert Code]. Act as the grading engineer. Did I miss any obvious edge cases, ignore standard conventions, or over-engineer the solution? Provide a critique before I submit it.
proTip: Always have a second pair of 'eyes' check for readability and simplicity. Over-engineering is a common reason take-homes fail.

title: The Recruiter Translation Matrix
useCase: Decoding vague rejection emails or interview feedback.
promptText: I received this feedback from a recruiter after an interview: '[Insert Feedback, e.g., We are looking for someone with more end-to-end ownership]'. Translate this corporate jargon into plain English. What exactly did I fail to demonstrate during the interview, and how do I fix it for the next one?
proTip: Recruiters use polite language to soften the blow. This prompt helps you extract the actual actionable critique.

title: The Live Debugging Coach
useCase: Practicing the 'think-aloud' protocol for pair programming interviews.
promptText: Give me a piece of broken code in [Insert Language] containing a logical bug. I will read through it and 'think aloud' by typing my thought process step-by-step as I try to find the bug. Grade my communication skills. Am I explaining my hypothesis clearly before making changes?
proTip: In pair programming interviews, *how* you communicate your debugging process is often more important than fixing the bug immediately.

title: The 30-60-90 Day Plan Generator
useCase: Standing out in the final round with a concrete action plan.
promptText: I am in the final interview round for a [Insert Target Role] at [Insert Target Company]. Help me generate a realistic 30-60-90 day plan that I can present to the hiring manager. Focus on onboarding, delivering an early win, and taking ownership of a specific metric.
proTip: Bringing a 30-60-90 day plan to a final round shows immense proactivity and sets you apart from 99% of other candidates.

title: The Tech Stack Matchmaker
useCase: Choosing the absolute best tools for a new project before writing code.
promptText: I am building a [Insert Project, e.g., personal portfolio with a 3D model showcase]. My primary goals are fast loading times and ease of deployment. I am considering using [Insert Tools, e.g., React, Three.js, and Vercel]. Validate this tech stack. Are there better, more modern alternatives I should consider for this specific use case? What are the trade-offs?
proTip: Never choose a framework just because it's popular; choose it because it fits the specific problem you are solving.

title: The Database Schema Sculptor
useCase: Designing a bulletproof database relationship model.
promptText: I need to design the database schema for a [Insert Project, e.g., secure banking system]. The core entities are [Insert Entities, e.g., Users, Accounts, Transactions, and Loans]. Should I use a relational database (SQL) or NoSQL for this? Outline the schema with exact field names, data types, and explain the primary/foreign key relationships.
proTip: Fixing a bad database schema after users are already using your app is a nightmare. Get this right on day one.

title: The API Endpoint Architect
useCase: Planning a clean, RESTful backend interface.
promptText: I am designing the backend API for a [Insert Project, e.g., superhero movie hub or recipe website]. Map out the exact REST API endpoints I will need for basic CRUD operations. Include the HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), the required route paths, and a brief JSON example of the expected request/response payloads.
proTip: Treat your API documentation like a contract between your frontend and your backend.

title: The ML Pipeline Blueprint
useCase: Structuring a machine learning project from data collection to deployment.
promptText: I am building a [Insert ML Project, e.g., live emotion detection system or medicine prediction app]. Outline the end-to-end architecture pipeline. Detail the steps for data ingestion, preprocessing, model training, and how I should serve the final model via an API for real-time inference.
proTip: Machine learning isn't just about training the model; it's about how the model safely consumes data in production.

title: The Folder Structure Generator
useCase: Organizing your code repository professionally.
promptText: I am starting a new full-stack project using [Insert Frontend, e.g., React] and [Insert Backend, e.g., Node.js]. Generate an industry-standard, scalable directory and folder structure. Briefly explain the purpose of directories like 'controllers', 'middlewares', 'services', and 'utils'.
proTip: A clean folder structure makes it infinitely easier for open-source contributors or hiring managers to read your code.

title: The 3D Web Integrator
useCase: Planning how to render heavy 3D assets on the web without lagging.
promptText: I want to display complex 3D models (like robots and architecture created in Blender) on a website. Outline the architectural strategy to do this efficiently. Detail how I should export the models (GLTF vs OBJ), how to handle texture compression, and the best JavaScript libraries to use for rendering and camera controls.
proTip: Web 3D is all about optimization. Focus heavily on reducing draw calls and compressing textures.

title: The System Scaler
useCase: Planning for massive traffic spikes.
promptText: My app, a [Insert App Type, e.g., live IPL match prediction platform], works fine for 100 users. However, during the finals, it might hit 100,000 concurrent users. Identify the most likely architectural bottlenecks (e.g., database read locks, server memory). Suggest highly specific scaling strategies like read-replicas, load balancing, and edge caching.
proTip: Always design your system assuming your database will be the first thing to fail under heavy load.

title: The Authentication Flow Mapper
useCase: Securing user data and handling logins safely.
promptText: I need to implement secure user authentication for my application. Compare the architectural differences between using JSON Web Tokens (JWT) vs Session-based cookies. Which one is better suited for a [Insert Architecture Type, e.g., decoupled React frontend and Python backend]? Outline the exact login flow step-by-step.
proTip: Never roll your own cryptography. Always understand the flow before implementing standard security libraries.

title: The Asynchronous Task Manager
useCase: Handling heavy backend tasks without freezing the user interface.
promptText: My web app needs to process heavy tasks, like [Insert Task, e.g., processing a voice-to-text audio file or rendering a video]. I cannot have the user stare at a loading spinner for 5 minutes. Architect a solution using a message broker (like Redis/RabbitMQ) and worker processes. Explain how the frontend will know when the task is complete.
proTip: Offloading heavy computation to background workers is the secret to a snappy, responsive user experience.

title: The MVP Scope Reducer
useCase: Cutting through feature-creep to actually launch your project.
promptText: I have a massive idea for a [Insert Idea, e.g., ultimate game hub with multiplayer, leaderboards, chat, and VR support]. Act as a strict Product Manager. Strip this down to the absolute Minimum Viable Product (MVP). What are the top 3 core features I MUST build first to prove the concept, and what should be pushed to Version 2?
proTip: Feature creep kills side projects. Ship the simplest version first, then iterate.

title: The Real-Time WebSockets Guide
useCase: Architecting applications that require instant data updates.
promptText: I am building a feature that requires live updates, such as a [Insert Feature, e.g., live chat in a game hub or live stock tickers]. Explain the architectural difference between short-polling, long-polling, Server-Sent Events (SSE), and WebSockets. Which protocol is strictly the best for my specific use case and why?
proTip: WebSockets are powerful but resource-intensive. Only keep connections open when absolutely necessary.

title: The State Management Strategist
useCase: Deciding how data flows through a complex frontend.
promptText: I am building a heavy frontend application in [Insert Framework, e.g., React]. The app has complex data like user profiles, dark mode settings, and cart items. Should I use native Context API, or do I need a strict state management library like Redux or Zustand? Map out the global state tree.
proTip: Avoid 'prop drilling' early on, but don't overcomplicate with Redux if your app only has a few pages.

title: The CI/CD Pipeline Planner
useCase: Automating your testing and deployment process.
promptText: I want to set up Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) for my [Insert Tech Stack] project using GitHub Actions. Outline the steps the pipeline should take every time I push code to the 'main' branch (e.g., linting, running unit tests, building, deploying to production).
proTip: Automating deployments removes human error and allows you to ship code faster and more confidently.

title: The Caching Optimizer
useCase: Drastically improving response times and reducing database costs.
promptText: My application makes frequent database queries for data that rarely changes (like [Insert Data, e.g., a list of superhero movies or static recipe categories]). Architect a caching layer using a tool like Redis. Explain cache invalidation—how and when should the cache update if the underlying database changes?
proTip: There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.

title: The Security Threat Modeler
useCase: Thinking like a hacker to protect your architecture.
promptText: Look at my proposed architecture: [Insert Architecture]. Conduct a basic threat modeling exercise. Identify the top 3 biggest security vulnerabilities (e.g., unvalidated inputs, exposed API keys, cross-site scripting) and architect structural defenses to mitigate them before I write the code.
proTip: Security is not an add-on you patch in at the end; it must be baked into the architecture from day one.

title: The Third-Party API Integrator
useCase: Designing resilient systems when relying on external services.
promptText: My app relies heavily on a third-party API for [Insert Function, e.g., fetching live cricket scores or processing payments]. How should I architect my backend to handle situations where their API goes down, rate-limits me, or takes 10 seconds to respond? Explain the concept of 'circuit breakers' and fallback data.
proTip: Never let an external service's downtime cause your entire application to crash.

title: The Microservices vs. Monolith Debater
useCase: Making the most debated architectural decision in software.
promptText: I am designing a new platform that handles [Insert Core Functions]. Give me a strict, objective comparison of building this as a single Monolith versus breaking it into Microservices. Focus on the trade-offs regarding deployment complexity, debugging, and team scaling. Which one is best for a solo developer vs. a team of 50?
proTip: Unless you have a massive team and clear domain boundaries, always start with a well-structured monolith.

title: The Cloud Infrastructure Cost Estimator
useCase: Preventing surprise $500 AWS bills at the end of the month.
promptText: I am planning to deploy my architecture on [Insert Cloud Provider, e.g., AWS / Google Cloud]. It consists of a web server, a managed PostgreSQL database, and cloud storage for user-uploaded files. Assuming roughly 10,000 monthly active users, provide a rough cost estimation breakdown. What hidden data transfer or bandwidth fees should I watch out for?
proTip: Cloud providers make their money on the things you forget to turn off or fail to optimize.

title: The Disaster Recovery Planner
useCase: Preparing for the absolute worst-case scenario.
promptText: Imagine my primary database server for [Insert Project] just permanently crashed and the data was wiped. Architect a disaster recovery plan. How frequently should I be running automated backups? Where should they be stored? How long should it take to restore the system to full operational status (RTO/RPO)?
proTip: A backup isn't a backup until you have successfully tested restoring from it.

title: The Edge Case Architecture Review
useCase: Finding the structural flaws in your logic.
promptText: Here is the flow of my application: [Describe the user flow and backend logic]. Challenge my architecture. What happens if a user double-clicks the 'Submit Payment' button? What happens if the internet drops halfway through an image upload? Help me design idempotent endpoints to handle these edge cases safely.
proTip: Designing idempotent APIs ensures that if a request is accidentally duplicated, the system state remains consistent and safe.

title: The Blank Canvas Constrainer
useCase: Breaking through creative block by forcing artificial limitations.
promptText: I need to design a [Insert Project Type, e.g., concert poster / 3D character] but I have severe creative block. Give me 3 highly specific, unconventional constraints. For example, dictate a bizarre color palette, a specific shape language I must use exclusively, or a weird theme I have to incorporate.
proTip: Creativity thrives on constraints. Having infinite options is what causes blank-page paralysis.

title: The UX Wireframe Architect
useCase: Planning the layout and user flow of a new app screen.
promptText: I am designing the [Insert Screen Name, e.g., checkout page or user dashboard] for a [Insert App Type, e.g., fitness tracking app]. List out the exact UI components I need on this screen from top to bottom. Prioritize them based on visual hierarchy and user goals. What is the primary Call to Action (CTA)?
proTip: Never start pushing pixels in Figma until you know exactly what information needs to be on the screen.

title: The 3D Topology Checker
useCase: Ensuring a 3D model deforms properly during animation.
promptText: I am modeling a [Insert Object/Character Part, e.g., human hand or car fender] in [Insert Software, e.g., Blender/Maya]. Outline the best practices for edge flow and topology for this specific object. Where should I place edge loops to ensure it deforms cleanly without pinching when rigged and animated?
proTip: Bad topology will ruin a great sculpt the second you try to move it. Plan your edge loops early.

title: The Render Time Reducer
useCase: Optimizing 3D scenes so they don't take 40 hours to render.
promptText: My scene in [Insert Render Engine, e.g., Cycles / Arnold] is taking way too long to render. It features [Describe Scene, e.g., a dark room with volumetric fog and glass materials]. Give me a checklist of 5 specific render settings or material hacks I can tweak to drastically reduce render times without losing noticeable visual quality.
proTip: In production, rendering is about cheating reality, not simulating it perfectly. Use optimization tricks.

title: The Color Theory Consultant
useCase: Generating meaningful, accessible color palettes.
promptText: I am designing a brand identity for a [Insert Industry/Vibe, e.g., high-end organic coffee shop]. I want the mood to feel [Insert Adjectives, e.g., warm, sophisticated, and earthy]. Generate a 5-color palette (with HEX codes). Explain exactly why these colors work together psychologically and ensure the primary text/background colors pass WCAG accessibility standards.
proTip: Accessible design is good design. Never use low-contrast colors for essential text.

title: The Typography Matchmaker
useCase: Pairing fonts that actually look good together.
promptText: I am working on a [Insert Project, e.g., modern tech blog or wedding invitation]. Suggest 3 different font pairings (Heading font + Body font). For each pair, explain the typographic contrast (e.g., serif vs sans-serif, varying weights) and why it fits the mood of my project. Only suggest free fonts from Google Fonts.
proTip: Limit yourself to two fonts maximum per project. Let weight and scale create the hierarchy.

title: The Figma Auto-Layout Strategist
useCase: Building scalable, responsive UI components.
promptText: I need to build a complex UI component in Figma: a [Insert Component, e.g., responsive pricing card with a bulleted list and a button]. Explain exactly how I should structure the Auto-Layout frames (rows, columns, fill container vs hug contents) so that the card scales perfectly whether viewed on mobile or desktop.
proTip: Mastering Auto-Layout separates junior designers from senior designers.

title: The UX Empathy Writer
useCase: Fixing robotic or frustrating error messages.
promptText: My app currently displays this error message: [Insert Current Message, e.g., 'Error 404: Database Connection Failed']. Rewrite this microcopy to be empathetic, helpful, and human. The tone of my brand is [Insert Tone, e.g., playful / highly professional]. Give me 3 variations.
proTip: Good UX writing guides the user out of a problem instead of just blaming them for it.

title: The UV Mapping Guide
useCase: Making the most tedious part of 3D modeling painless.
promptText: I have finished modeling a [Insert Complex Object, e.g., detailed sci-fi rifle] and I need to UV unwrap it. Walk me through the logical strategy for placing seams. Where should I hide the seams, and how should I pack the UV islands to maximize texel density for the most visible parts of the model?
proTip: Always hide your seams where the camera (or the player) will never look.

title: The Lighting Studio Architect
useCase: Creating cinematic lighting setups for 3D or photography.
promptText: I need to light a [Insert Subject, e.g., realistic portrait / product render of a glass bottle] in a 3D environment to make it look cinematic. Give me a detailed lighting setup. Where should I place the key light, fill light, and rim light? What color temperatures and intensities should I use to create a [Insert Mood, e.g., moody and dramatic] vibe?
proTip: Lighting is 80% of what makes a 3D render look realistic. Flat lighting makes great models look terrible.

title: The Motion Graphics Expression Generator
useCase: Automating animations in After Effects using math instead of keyframes.
promptText: I am working in After Effects and I want to animate a [Insert Object/Property, e.g., a shape layer's scale]. I want it to [Describe Motion, e.g., bounce dynamically and settle like a spring when it scales up]. Write the exact JavaScript expression I need to paste into the property to achieve this without manual keyframing.
proTip: Using expressions saves hours of tweaking keyframes and graph editors.

title: The Portfolio Case Study Structurer
useCase: Turning a simple visual project into an impressive Behance/Portfolio study.
promptText: I just finished a [Insert Project Type, e.g., UI redesign of Spotify]. I want to turn this into a comprehensive case study for my portfolio. Outline the sections I need to include (e.g., Problem Statement, User Research, Iteration). What specific deliverables should I show in each section to prove my thought process to recruiters?
proTip: Recruiters hire you for your problem-solving process, not just the final pretty picture.

title: The Video Pacing Consultant
useCase: Fixing a video edit that feels boring or slow.
promptText: I am editing a [Insert Video Type, e.g., 10-minute YouTube documentary or 30-second promo]. The rough cut is done, but the pacing feels dragging and I am losing the viewer's attention. Give me 5 advanced video editing techniques (like J/L cuts, b-roll timing, or sound design cues) to increase the perceived momentum and retention.
proTip: Pacing isn't just about cutting faster; it's about rhythm. Use audio to drive the visual cuts.

title: The Color Grading Strategist
useCase: Achieving a specific cinematic look in video post-production.
promptText: I am color grading footage shot on [Insert Camera/Profile, e.g., Sony S-Log3]. I want to achieve a [Insert Look, e.g., Cyberpunk neon / vintage 90s film] look. Walk me through the order of operations in [Insert Software, e.g., DaVinci Resolve]. How should I handle the color space transform, contrast curve, and HSL adjustments?
proTip: Always color correct (balance exposure and white balance) before you color grade (apply a creative look).

title: The UI Animation Easing Coach
useCase: Making UI interactions feel snappy and satisfying.
promptText: I am designing a UI animation for when a user [Insert Action, e.g., clicks a 'Submit' button and a modal pops up]. Linear animation feels robotic. Recommend the exact CSS cubic-bezier curves (e.g., ease-in-out, spring, bounce) I should use for the entrance and exit animations to make it feel [Insert Vibe, e.g., playful and tactile].
proTip: Entrance animations should generally be slightly slower and use 'ease-out', while exit animations should be faster and use 'ease-in'.

title: The UX Research Question Crafter
useCase: Asking users the right questions without biasing their answers.
promptText: I am conducting user interviews for a new [Insert App Concept, e.g., student budgeting app]. I want to know if they would actually use it. Generate 5 open-ended, non-leading questions that will reveal their actual habits and pain points, rather than just asking them 'Do you like this idea?'
proTip: Users will always lie and say your idea is good to be polite. Ask about their past behavior, not their future intent.

title: The Asset Naming Convention Enforcer
useCase: Organizing massive creative projects so teammates don't hate you.
promptText: I am working on a massive [Insert Software, e.g., Photoshop / Unity] project with hundreds of layers/assets. Propose a strict, professional naming convention for my files and layers. How should I denote versions, asset types, and states (like hover vs active)? Give me 5 examples.
proTip: Never name a file 'Final_v2_ActuallyFinal.psd'. Establish a version control naming rule on day one.

title: The Creative Brief Simulator
useCase: Generating realistic projects to build your portfolio.
promptText: I want to build my portfolio. Act as a demanding client. Generate a realistic, comprehensive creative brief for a [Insert Project Type, e.g., mobile app design for a local plant nursery]. Include the target audience, business goals, mandatory features, technical constraints, and a specific stylistic requirement.
proTip: Treat this simulated brief as seriously as a real paying client to make your portfolio look highly professional.

title: The Logo Scalability Auditor
useCase: Ensuring brand designs work in the real world.
promptText: I have designed a logo that features [Describe Logo, e.g., a detailed illustration of a tree with thin typography]. Critique this design strictly on scalability and versatility. What will happen to these details when the logo is shrunk down to a 16x16 pixel website favicon or embroidered on a shirt? How should I adapt it?
proTip: A great logo works just as well stamped in black and white as it does in full color on a billboard.

title: The Compositing Logic Checker
useCase: Making photoshopped images or VFX shots look seamlessly real.
promptText: I am compositing a [Insert Element, e.g., a 3D spaceship] into a live-action background plate of a [Insert Background, e.g., sunny city street]. List the 5 critical visual elements I need to match exactly (like black levels, grain, light direction, focal blur) so the fake element doesn't look pasted on.
proTip: Always match the black levels of your CGI to the darkest shadow in the real-world plate.

title: The Formula Architect
useCase: Translating plain English into complex Excel or Google Sheets formulas.
promptText: Act as an expert data analyst. I am using [Spreadsheet Software, e.g., Excel, Google Sheets]. I have a dataset where Column A is [Column A Data] and Column B is [Column B Data]. Write a formula to [Describe the desired calculation or output]. Explain how the formula works step-by-step.
proTip: Specify your software because Excel and Google Sheets have slightly different function libraries (like FILTER or XLOOKUP).

title: The VLOOKUP / XLOOKUP Fixer
useCase: Debugging broken lookup formulas.
promptText: My [Formula Type, e.g., VLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH] is returning an error. My current formula is [Insert Formula]. I am trying to search for [Search Value] inside [Target Range] to return the value in [Return Column]. Tell me exactly why it is breaking and give me the corrected formula.
proTip: Often, errors are caused by mismatched data types (text vs. numbers). Ask the AI to include a TRIM or VALUE wrap if needed.

title: The Data Cleaner
useCase: Formatting messy, raw data exports.
promptText: I have a messy column of data that looks like this: [Paste a few rows of messy data]. I need to extract just the [Specific Data to Extract, e.g., email domains, zip codes]. Write an Excel/Google Sheets formula to extract this cleanly, and account for blank cells.
proTip: If formulas are too complex, ask the AI to generate a quick Regex pattern or VBA/App Script instead.

title: The Pivot Table Planner
useCase: Structuring raw data for executive summaries.
promptText: I have a dataset with the following headers: [Paste Headers]. I need to answer this business question: [Insert Business Question]. Tell me exactly how to set up my Pivot Table. What should go into the Rows, Columns, Values, and Filters boxes?
proTip: Ask the AI to recommend the best chart type (e.g., bar chart, line graph) to accompany this specific Pivot Table.

title: The SQL Query Generator
useCase: Writing accurate SQL queries from plain English requirements.
promptText: Act as a Senior Data Engineer. I am using [SQL Dialect, e.g., PostgreSQL, MySQL]. I have a table named [Table Name] with these columns: [List Columns]. Write a query to find the [Desired Output, e.g., top 5 customers by revenue this month]. Include comments explaining the logic.
proTip: Always provide the exact table and column names so you can copy-paste the result without editing.

title: The SQL Query Optimizer
useCase: Speeding up slow-running database queries.
promptText: Review this SQL query: [Paste SQL Query]. It is running too slowly on my [SQL Dialect] database. Identify any performance bottlenecks (like N+1 queries or missing indexes) and rewrite it to be highly optimized.
proTip: If using EXPLAIN ANALYZE, paste the output plan into the prompt for hyper-specific tuning advice.

title: The Python Pandas Translator
useCase: Converting spreadsheet logic into Python code.
promptText: I normally use Excel to [Describe Excel Workflow, e.g., filter rows where sales > 100 and group by region]. How do I do this exact same thing in Python using the pandas library? My dataframe is called [Dataframe Name].
proTip: Pandas can be tricky with chained indexing. Ask the AI to provide the most 'Pythonic' and efficient method.

title: The Regex Pattern Builder
useCase: Creating regular expressions for data extraction.
promptText: I need a Regular Expression (Regex) pattern to extract [What you want to extract, e.g., US phone numbers] from a messy string. The flavor of Regex I am using is [Language/Tool, e.g., Python, Google Sheets]. Provide the pattern and explain what each symbol does.
proTip: Always provide 3 examples of what the text looks like so the AI can test its own pattern before giving it to you.

title: The Storytelling Analyst
useCase: Extracting the 'So What?' from a block of numbers.
promptText: Here are the key metrics from our recent [Project/Campaign Name]: [Paste Data Summary]. Act as a Data Storyteller. Summarize this data in 3 bullet points for a non-technical executive. Focus on the business impact and what action we should take next.
proTip: Executives don't care about the math; they care about the money. Ask the AI to focus heavily on ROI.

title: The Conditional Formatting Coder
useCase: Writing custom formulas for cell highlighting.
promptText: I am in [Software]. I want to use Conditional Formatting on Column [Target Column]. Write the custom formula rule that will highlight the cell ONLY IF [Describe Condition, e.g., the date is past due AND the status is not 'Complete'].
proTip: Make sure to tell the AI if you want the whole row highlighted or just the single cell.

title: The VBA / Macro Scripter
useCase: Automating repetitive Excel tasks without knowing how to code.
promptText: Write an Excel VBA script that will [Describe the repetitive task, e.g., loop through all sheets, copy data from A1:D10, and paste it into a master sheet]. Add comments to every line so I know what it does.
proTip: Always save a backup of your workbook before running AI-generated VBA scripts!

title: The Google Apps Script Generator
useCase: Automating Google Workspace.
promptText: Write a Google Apps Script that triggers when [Trigger Event, e.g., a new row is added]. The script should [Describe Action, e.g., send an email to the address in Column C with the subject 'Welcome'].
proTip: You can ask the AI to generate HTML templates to make the automated emails look professional.

title: The DAX Measure Creator
useCase: Building Power BI calculations.
promptText: I am working in Power BI. I need a DAX measure to calculate [Calculation Goal, e.g., Year-over-Year Sales Growth]. My fact table is called [Fact Table] and my date table is called [Date Table].
proTip: DAX relies heavily on context. Make sure to mention if you need this calculated at a row level or aggregate level.

title: The A/B Test Evaluator
useCase: Determining if data results are statistically significant.
promptText: I ran an A/B test. Variant A had [Number] visitors and [Number] conversions. Variant B had [Number] visitors and [Number] conversions. Calculate the conversion rates, tell me if the result is statistically significant at a 95% confidence level, and explain what that means.
proTip: You can ask the AI to format the output as a formal report to copy-paste directly to your marketing team.

title: The Dashboard Wireframer
useCase: Planning a BI dashboard layout before building it.
promptText: I need to build a dashboard in [Tool, e.g., Tableau, Looker] for [Target Audience, e.g., the VP of Sales]. The goal of the dashboard is [Goal]. Suggest 4 high-level KPI scorecards for the top, and 3 specific charts/graphs for the main body. Explain why each chart is necessary.
proTip: Visual hierarchy is key. Ask the AI what colors should be used to draw attention to critical metrics.

title: The Dataset Joiner
useCase: Figuring out the logic for merging two messy data sources.
promptText: I have Dataset 1 with columns [List Columns 1]. I have Dataset 2 with columns [List Columns 2]. I need to merge them to analyze [Analysis Goal]. What is the best 'key' to join these on? Should I use a Left Join, Inner Join, or Outer Join? Explain why.
proTip: If the keys don't match perfectly (e.g., 'Apple Inc.' vs 'Apple'), ask the AI for fuzzy matching strategies.

title: The Anomaly Detective
useCase: Finding outliers in a dataset.
promptText: I am analyzing [Type of Data, e.g., daily website traffic] and need to find outliers. What are 3 statistical methods or formulas I can use in [Software, e.g., Excel, Python] to automatically flag anomalies?
proTip: Standard deviation and Interquartile Range (IQR) are usually the best places to start.

title: The KPI Brainstormer
useCase: Figuring out what metrics actually matter.
promptText: I manage a [Type of Business/Department, e.g., SaaS Customer Success team]. Give me a list of 5 actionable lagging indicators and 5 actionable leading indicators I should be tracking in my spreadsheets. Define the formula for each.
proTip: Leading indicators predict the future; lagging indicators report the past. Both are necessary.

title: The Synthetic Data Generator
useCase: Creating dummy data to test formulas or database schemas.
promptText: Generate a CSV format table with [Number] rows of realistic dummy data for a [Industry/Niche] company. Include the following columns: [List Desired Columns]. Make sure the data follows logical constraints (e.g., end dates are after start dates).
proTip: Paste this directly into a plain text file, save it as a .csv, and open it in Excel to start testing immediately.

title: The Code to Plain English Translator
useCase: Understanding a massive script left behind by a former employee.
promptText: I inherited this [Language, e.g., SQL, Python, R] script from a former coworker. I don't know this language well. Explain exactly what this script is doing in plain English, step-by-step: [Paste Code].
proTip: Ask the AI to rewrite the script adding inline comments so you never forget what it does.

title: The Writer's Block Breaker
useCase: Getting past the blank page syndrome with strong opening hooks.
promptText: Act as an expert copywriter. I need to write a [Format, e.g., blog post, email, landing page] about [Topic]. I am stuck and don't know how to start. Give me 3 highly engaging, completely different opening hooks to get the reader's attention immediately. The tone should be [Tone].
proTip: If you don't like the hooks, ask the AI to make them 'more punchy', 'more academic', or 'more controversial'.

title: The Tone Mimic
useCase: Making AI sound like a specific brand, author, or persona.
promptText: Analyze the writing style, tone, and sentence structure of this text: [Insert Reference Text]. Then, write a [Format, e.g., Twitter thread, product description] about [New Topic] using that exact same style and voice.
proTip: The longer the reference text you provide, the better the AI will adapt to the specific cadence and vocabulary.

title: The Cold Email Converter
useCase: Writing B2B outreach emails that actually get replies.
promptText: Write a short, punchy cold email to [Target Audience/Job Title]. The goal is to get them to [Desired Action, e.g., book a 10-minute demo, reply to a question]. Use the 'Problem-Agitate-Solve' (PAS) framework. Mention our core value proposition: [Insert Value Prop]. Keep it under 150 words.
proTip: Always ask the AI to provide 3 different subject line options for A/B testing.

title: The SEO Blog Outliner
useCase: Structuring an article to rank on Google before writing it.
promptText: I am writing an SEO blog post targeting the primary keyword '[Primary Keyword]'. The target audience is [Target Audience]. Generate a comprehensive outline including an H1, multiple H2s, and H3s. Include a list of LSI (Latent Semantic Indexing) keywords I should sprinkle throughout the text.
proTip: Use the outline as a skeleton, then ask the AI to write the post one H2 section at a time for better quality.

title: The Headline Hook Generator
useCase: Brainstorming clickable, high-converting titles.
promptText: I have written a [Content Type, e.g., YouTube video, Article, Ad] about [Topic]. Generate 10 highly clickable, curiosity-inducing headlines. Do not use clickbait, but make them impossible to ignore. Use formats like 'How to...', 'The Secret to...', and numbered lists.
proTip: Numbers in headlines (especially odd numbers) statistically increase click-through rates.

title: The Landing Page Transformer
useCase: Structuring high-converting website copy.
promptText: I am building a landing page for [Product/Service Name], which helps [Target Audience] achieve [Main Benefit]. Write the copy for the page using the AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action) framework. Include a Hero Headline, a Sub-headline, 3 key feature/benefit bullets, and a Call to Action.
proTip: Features tell, benefits sell. Ask the AI to ensure every feature is tied directly to an emotional benefit.

title: The Grammar & Flow Polisher
useCase: Editing rough drafts for clarity, punchiness, and rhythm.
promptText: Review the following text: [Insert Rough Draft]. Fix any grammatical errors, but more importantly, improve the flow and readability. Make the sentences punchier, remove passive voice, and eliminate filler words. Show me the revised version and briefly explain what you changed.
proTip: Ask the AI to format the output at a '7th-grade reading level' to ensure maximum readability for a general audience.

title: The Metaphor Maker
useCase: Explaining complex or boring concepts using relatable analogies.
promptText: I need to explain the concept of [Complex Concept, e.g., blockchain, APIs, compound interest] to [Target Audience, e.g., a 5-year-old, a non-technical CEO]. Generate 3 creative metaphors or analogies that make this concept instantly understandable.
proTip: Metaphors are the ultimate cheat code for persuasive writing. Use them in your hero sections and pitch decks.

title: The Twitter/X Thread Weaver
useCase: Turning long-form ideas into viral social media threads.
promptText: Turn this core idea into a compelling, 7-part Twitter/X thread: [Insert Core Idea/Text]. The first tweet must be a strong hook that creates a knowledge gap. The final tweet must have a clear call-to-action (CTA). Keep the tone [Tone, e.g., authoritative, conversational].
proTip: Format matters on X. Ask the AI to include line breaks and avoid using excessive emojis or hashtags.

title: The Product Description Seller
useCase: Writing e-commerce copy that drives add-to-carts.
promptText: Write a compelling product description for a [Product Name/Type]. The key features are [List Features]. The target buyer struggles with [Customer Pain Point]. Focus heavily on sensory words and the emotional transformation the product provides.
proTip: Include a section for 'Who this is NOT for' to build trust and increase conversion rates among your true target audience.

title: The Newsletter Nurturer
useCase: Drafting engaging weekly emails to your subscribers.
promptText: Write a weekly newsletter for an audience interested in [Niche/Topic]. The main story/lesson this week is [Main Lesson]. Include a brief intro, the main value-add section, and a 'Resource of the week' shoutout. Make it feel personal, like a letter from a friend.
proTip: Use the 'P.S.' section at the bottom—it's statistically the most read part of any marketing email.

title: The LinkedIn Thought Leader
useCase: Creating professional, story-driven networking posts.
promptText: Write a LinkedIn post about a time I learned a hard lesson regarding [Topic, e.g., leadership, failure, coding]. Use short, one-sentence paragraphs for readability. Start with a contrarian statement or a vulnerable admission. End with a question to drive comments.
proTip: LinkedIn algorithms love dwell time. Start with a hook that forces people to click 'See more...'.

title: The Objection Overcomer
useCase: Pre-emptively answering customer doubts in your copy.
promptText: I am selling a [Product/Service] for [Price]. The biggest objections my customers have are [List Objections, e.g., it's too expensive, it takes too much time]. Write a FAQ section or a 'Guarantee' section for my sales page that completely dismantles these objections.
proTip: Reframe price objections into an 'investment' or compare the cost to a relatable daily expense (like a cup of coffee).

title: The Press Release Pro
useCase: Drafting official company announcements for journalists.
promptText: Write a formal press release announcing [Company Name]'s new [Product/Milestone/Partnership]. Include a strong headline, a dateline, an opening summary paragraph, a quote from our CEO [CEO Name], and a boilerplate 'About the Company' section at the end.
proTip: Journalists are busy. Keep the 'inverted pyramid' structure—put the most crucial information in the very first paragraph.

title: The Video Script Hook
useCase: Scripting the first 15 seconds of a YouTube/TikTok video.
promptText: I am making a short-form video about [Video Topic]. Write a 15-second script for the intro. Do not say 'Hi guys' or introduce yourself. Start immediately with a shocking fact, a visual pattern interrupt, or a bold promise that forces them to keep watching.
proTip: Include visual cues in brackets (e.g., [Zoom in fast], [Show graphic]) so the AI helps you direct the video too.

title: The Jargon Translator
useCase: Turning dense, technical jargon into human language.
promptText: Translate this highly technical paragraph into plain English that a high schooler could understand, without losing the core meaning: [Insert Technical Text].
proTip: Great for rewriting terms of service, developer documentation, or medical/legal texts for a consumer audience.

title: The Call-To-Action (CTA) Optimizer
useCase: Generating button copy that begs to be clicked.
promptText: My current button copy says 'Submit' (or 'Click Here'). The user is clicking it to get [Describe What They Get, e.g., a free PDF, a consultation]. Generate 10 highly specific, action-oriented CTA button texts that focus on the value they are about to receive.
proTip: Best practice: The button text should complete the sentence 'I want to...' (e.g., 'I want to [Get My Free Guide]').

title: The Case Study Storyteller
useCase: Formatting client success stories for B2B sales.
promptText: Turn these raw notes into a compelling B2B case study. Client: [Client Name]. Problem: [Problem]. Solution: [Our Solution]. Results: [Metrics/Results]. Format it with clear headings: The Challenge, The Solution, and The Impact. Include a placeholder for a pull-quote.
proTip: Numbers speak louder than words. Ensure the AI highlights specific percentages, time saved, or revenue generated.

title: The Ad Copy A/B Tester
useCase: Generating distinct variations for Facebook or Google Ads.
promptText: I am running Facebook Ads for [Product/Service]. Write 3 completely different ad variations. Variation 1 should focus on logical benefits (saving time/money). Variation 2 should focus on emotional pain points (fear of missing out/stress). Variation 3 should be a short, punchy testimonial style.
proTip: Ensure the AI keeps the primary text under 125 characters so it doesn't get truncated on mobile screens.

title: The Crisis Communicator
useCase: Drafting an apology or damage-control email to customers.
promptText: We experienced a major issue: [Describe Issue, e.g., site went down for 12 hours, orders were delayed]. Write a sincere, transparent apology email to our customers. Take extreme ownership, explain what happened without making excuses, and detail the exact steps we are taking to ensure it never happens again.
proTip: Sincerity is everything. Instruct the AI to avoid corporate-speak like 'We apologize for any inconvenience'.

title: The Task Triage (Eisenhower Matrix)
useCase: Instantly prioritizing a chaotic and overwhelming to-do list.
promptText: Act as an executive productivity coach. Here is my completely unorganized list of tasks for the week: [Insert Task List]. Organize these into an Eisenhower Matrix (1. Do First, 2. Schedule, 3. Delegate, 4. Delete). Tell me exactly what I should do in the next 60 minutes to gain momentum.
proTip: Don't filter yourself when pasting the list. Include personal chores alongside work tasks so the AI sees your full mental load.

title: The Micro-Step Breakdown
useCase: Defeating procrastination by breaking massive projects into tiny steps.
promptText: I have a massive project to complete: [Project Goal]. It feels overwhelming and I am avoiding it. Break this down into 10 incredibly small, actionable 'micro-steps' that take less than [Number of Minutes] minutes each. Make the very first step ridiculously easy.
proTip: A good first micro-step should take less than 2 minutes, like 'Create a new folder on the desktop' or 'Open a blank document'.

title: The Time-Block Scheduler
useCase: Converting a raw to-do list into a realistic daily calendar.
promptText: I need to plan my day using time-blocking. I have [Number of Hours] hours available starting at [Start Time]. Here are my tasks and estimated durations: [List Tasks and Times]. I also need a [Lunch/Break Length] minute break. Generate a chronological schedule for my day, grouping similar tasks together.
proTip: Always over-estimate how long tasks take by 20% to give yourself a buffer for interruptions.

title: The 80/20 Analyzer (Pareto Principle)
useCase: Identifying the few tasks that will drive the most results.
promptText: Here is a list of everything I am currently working on or planning to do: [Insert Project/Task List]. Based on the 80/20 rule (Pareto Principle), identify the 20% of these tasks that are likely to yield 80% of the positive results for my main goal of [Main Goal]. Tell me what I should ruthlessly cut.
proTip: This is highly effective for freelancers and founders who are wearing too many hats.

title: The SMART Goal Sculptor
useCase: Turning a vague ambition into a concrete, measurable plan.
promptText: I have a vague goal: [Vague Goal, e.g., 'Get better at coding' or 'Grow my business']. Turn this into a strict SMART goal (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound). Then, give me 3 milestones to track my progress over the next [Timeframe, e.g., 90 days].
proTip: If the goal feels too easy after it's made SMART, ask the AI to '10X the ambition' of the goal.

title: The Energy-Based Workflow
useCase: Matching your tasks to your natural daily energy levels.
promptText: I want to organize my tasks based on my energy levels. My high-energy peak is during the [Time of Day, e.g., Morning], and I crash during the [Crash Time, e.g., Mid-afternoon]. Sort this list of tasks into 'Deep Work' (high energy), 'Shallow Work' (medium energy), and 'Brain-Dead Work' (low energy): [Insert Tasks].
proTip: Save email replies, data entry, and organizing files for your 'Brain-Dead' low-energy windows.

title: The Habit Loop Architect
useCase: Designing a new, sticky habit using psychology.
promptText: I want to build a new daily habit of [Desired Habit]. Using Charles Duhigg's Habit Loop framework, help me design an obvious 'Cue', an easy 'Routine', and a satisfying 'Reward' to make this stick. Also, suggest an existing habit I can 'stack' this onto.
proTip: Habit stacking (e.g., 'After I pour my morning coffee, I will do X') is statistically the best way to build a new routine.

title: The Distraction Shield (If-Then Plan)
useCase: Pre-planning your response to inevitable interruptions.
promptText: I am trying to focus on [Deep Work Task]. However, I constantly get distracted by [List Distractions, e.g., phone notifications, coworkers, wandering thoughts]. Create a strict 'If-Then' implementation intention plan for each of these distractions so I know exactly how to react when they happen.
proTip: Pre-making decisions reduces cognitive load. When the distraction happens, you just follow the script.

title: The Meeting Agenda Architect
useCase: Designing a hyper-efficient meeting to prevent wasted time.
promptText: I have to lead a [Length of Meeting] minute meeting about [Meeting Topic] with [List Attendees/Roles]. The final decision we MUST make by the end of this meeting is [Desired Outcome]. Draft a strict, minute-by-minute agenda that prevents us from getting off-track.
proTip: Include a 5-minute 'parking lot' section at the end for off-topic ideas that come up during the discussion.

title: The Async Update Generator
useCase: Replacing a useless status meeting with a clear text update.
promptText: I want to cancel an upcoming status meeting and send an asynchronous update instead. Turn these rough notes into a highly scannable, professional update: What I did: [Notes on past work]. What I'm doing next: [Notes on future work]. Blockers/Needs: [Notes on what's holding you up].
proTip: Use bullet points and bold text for names to ensure people actually read it.

title: The 'Saying No' Script
useCase: Politely declining requests to protect your time.
promptText: A [Relationship, e.g., coworker, boss, friend] asked me to [The Request]. I don't have the time or bandwidth to do this, but I want to maintain a great relationship. Write 3 different scripts to politely decline: one direct, one offering a compromise, and one referring them to someone else.
proTip: Never use the word 'sorry' when protecting your time. Use 'I appreciate you thinking of me, but...' instead.

title: The Delegation Matrix
useCase: Figuring out exactly what to hand off to a team member or VA.
promptText: I am overwhelmed. Here are my current responsibilities: [List Responsibilities]. I have a [Role, e.g., Junior Dev, Virtual Assistant] who can help me. Identify which tasks I should delegate immediately, which I should automate, and which I absolutely must keep for myself.
proTip: The rule of thumb: Delegate anything that someone else can do 70% as well as you can.

title: The Weekly Review Guide
useCase: Conducting a personal review to close out the week cleanly.
promptText: Act as an accountability partner. I want to do a weekly review. Ask me 5 deep, reflective questions one at a time to help me analyze what went right this week regarding my goal of [Goal], what went wrong, and how I can optimize my schedule for next week. Wait for my answer before asking the next question.
proTip: Doing this on Friday afternoon prevents work anxiety from bleeding into your weekend.

title: The Skill Acquisition Roadmap
useCase: Learning a new skill rapidly using the 20-hour framework.
promptText: I want to learn how to [Skill, e.g., edit videos in Premiere Pro, speak basic Spanish]. I have 20 hours to dedicate to this over the next month. Deconstruct this skill into the 4-5 most crucial sub-skills I need to practice to see the fastest results, ignoring the advanced theory.
proTip: Most people quit learning because they start with theory. Ask the AI to give you a 'hands-on project' for hour 1.

title: The Context-Switching Minimizer
useCase: Batching similar tasks to reduce cognitive fatigue.
promptText: Context switching is ruining my focus. Here is a list of all my random tasks for the week: [Insert Tasks]. Group these tasks into specific 'Batches' (e.g., Communication, Deep Work, Errands, Admin) so I can tackle them in focused sprints rather than bouncing back and forth.
proTip: Schedule your 'Communication Batch' (emails/Slacks) to only happen twice a day, rather than keeping the tabs open.

title: The Project Post-Mortem
useCase: Extracting lessons learned after completing a big project.
promptText: We just finished a major project: [Project Name]. The things that went well were [Successes]. The things that failed or caused stress were [Failures]. Generate a formal 'Post-Mortem' report summarizing these points and providing 3 actionable systems we can implement to avoid those failures next time.
proTip: Focus strictly on the system, not the person. Say 'The QA process failed' instead of 'John messed up'.

title: The OKR Draftsman
useCase: Setting quarterly Objectives and Key Results for a team.
promptText: Our team's main objective for this quarter is to [High Level Objective, e.g., Improve Customer Retention]. Generate 3-4 measurable, quantitative Key Results (KRs) that will prove we have achieved this objective. Make them ambitious but tracking-friendly.
proTip: A good OKR should make you slightly uncomfortable. Aim for a 70% completion rate.

title: The Routine Optimizer
useCase: Designing a realistic morning or evening routine.
promptText: I want to build a [Morning/Evening] routine that takes exactly [Number of Minutes] minutes. My primary goals are to [Goals, e.g., wake up without snoozing, exercise, read]. Create a step-by-step timeline. Make it realistic for someone who struggles with [Personal Struggle, e.g., hitting snooze, late-night scrolling].
proTip: The secret to a good morning routine is actually a strict evening routine to prepare for the next day.

title: The Procrastination Psychologist
useCase: Getting to the root cause of why you are stuck.
promptText: I am severely procrastinating on [Task]. I know I need to do it, but I keep putting it off. Act as a behavioral psychologist. Ask me 3 probing questions to help me identify if my procrastination is driven by fear, perfectionism, lack of clarity, or burnout. Provide a tailored solution based on my answers.
proTip: Be completely honest with the AI. Sometimes just typing out *why* you are scared of a task diminishes the fear.

title: The Daily Brain Dump Organizer
